Everest claimed to have stolen 590 gigabytes of data that included “regional HR and learning exports, integration documentation, software components and PwC e-learning courses.”
The data contains information “about individuals and their organizational and employment history,” Everest said, including names, email addresses, telephone numbers, addresses and other details.

Customer satisfaction with total loss auto insurance claims fell for a third straight year, while satisfaction improved for claims involving repairable vehicles, a new study looking at this year shows.
Customer satisfaction with total loss claims fell 12 points on a 1,000-point scale in 2026, marking a 46-point decline since 2023, according to the JD Power 2026 U.S. Auto Claims Satisfaction Study.
However, satisfaction with claims involving repairable vehicles improved four points and overall auto claims customer satisfaction was unchanged from last year at 700.
Overall, 26% of auto insurance claims were classified as total losses this year, up from 16% four years ago. The growing share of total losses reflects rising vehicle repair costs, consumers keeping vehicles longer and higher deductibles removing smaller repairs from the claims process, according to the study. Affordability pressures also led some customers to drop rental coverage or increase deductibles, complicating the claims experience.
Repair cycle times have improved as claim volumes have declined and repair shops have more capacity. Average repair cycle times fell to 15.3 days in the first quarter of 2026, down 10 days from the first quarter of 2024, the study shows.
The study also found differences in customer satisfaction based on how effectively insurers communicate across channels. Satisfaction averaged 804 among customers who strongly agreed their insurers provided a seamless experience across communication channels, compared with 390 among customers who disagreed.
The study shows that insurers provided a seamless cross-channel experience 54% of the time, one of the lowest-performing measures in the study. Problems cited included unclear explanations, customers having to use multiple channels to get answers and digital tools that did not work as expected.
Amica ranked highest in overall customer satisfaction with a score of 775, followed by Nationwide at 743 and Automobile Club of Southern California (AAA) at 740.
The study examines auto claims experiences in order of importance: trust, fairness of settlement, people, time to settle claim, communication, ease of resolving claim, ease of starting claim and digital channels. The 2026 study was based on responses from 8,261 auto insurance customers who settled claims within the nine months before participating in the survey, which was conducted from September 2025 through August 2026.

These actions include a failure to enforce protections from toxic silica dust, removing staff who screen for black lung, cutting the number of mine inspectors, and failing to adequately compensate mining families impacted by black lung.
These actions stand in contrast to the Trump administration’s sizable investments and outspoken advocacy for bolstering the coal industry more broadly, the researchers contend.

The rise in illness may be showing up in more workers’ compensation claims. Nationwide, the number of claims has grown steadily in recent years. But the U.S. Department of Labor’s data show that federal black lung claims rose steadily in Kentucky, from 3,956 in 2013 to 4,776 in 2024, then dipped slightly to 4,734 last year. Benefits paid also grew steadily, topping $46 million last year.

The Delaware Supreme Court has upheld a Chancery Court ruling ordering Verisk Analytics Inc. to keep working on a $2.35 billion acquisition of roofing software maker AccuLynx.
Verisk tried to pull out of the deal last December after the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) notified it that it had not completed its review of the transaction by the termination date of December 26. AccuLynx went to court to force Verisk to complete the deal.
Verisk had announced its plan to acquire AccuLynx in July 2025 and initially said it expected to close by the third quarter of 2025. AccuLynx and Verisk believed that the merger presented only minimal antitrust risk, as the companies did not compete horizontally or have a vertical supplier-customer relationship.
After last week’s Delaware Supreme Court ruling, Verisk said that it would comply with the ruling but cannot guarantee that the merger will be finalized.
Acculynx objected to Verisk’s exit from their agreement, claiming Verisk was responsible for the FTC delay that it then tried to use to walk away from their merger agreement.
In August, Chancery Court Judge Bonnie David agreed with AccuLynx. The judge found that Verisk’s termination was invalid because Verisk’s own “willful conduct caused the failure of a condition to closing.”
Verisk had answered no when the FTC first asked whether Verisk had ever terminated integration discussions with an AccuLynx competitor or rejected a request for an enhanced integration. The FTC had information that Verisk had in fact done so with a company called ServiceTitan. So the FTC asked again and as a result of having to issue a second request told Verisk it could not meet a December 26 deadline for review. Days later, Verisk purported to terminate the merger agreement on the extended termination date.
Acculynx asked the court to order Verisk to honor the merger agreement, including by using reasonable efforts to obtain clearance by the FTC and to close the merger if the FTC approves the transaction. AccuLynx also asked for damages in the amount of $3.85 million, plus prejudgment interest.
The Chancery Court ruled that AccuLynx was entitled to the order of specific performance against Verisk. The court also approved the damages for AccuLynx, finding that Verisk had waived its right to oppose the damages.
The court noted that the parties specifically agreed in the merger agreement that a party could not terminate if its own “willful conduct” was the “primary cause” of the failure to satisfy a condition. “It is not inequitable to hold the parties to their bargain,” the judge stated.
Verisk objected to the performance order requiring it to pursue the deal, arguing in part that such a remedy was not available where damages would provide adequate relief.
However, the Chancery Court noted that in addition to any other rights and remedies, the merger agreement made it clear that AccuLynx as seller had the right to enforce the obligations of the buyer “not only by an action or actions for damages but also by an action or actions for specific performance, injunctive and/or other equitable relief.”
The judge directed the parties to submit a proposed form of final order to implement the ruling.
The Delaware Supreme Court did not elaborate beyond saying that the Chancery Court opinion should be affirmed on the basis of and for the reasons stated.

A lawsuit filed on Friday involving the pay practices of Chili’s operator Brinker International is seeking to strike down New York state’s lower minimum wage for workers who earn tips, which it claims fuels the sexual and racial harassment of workers.
The proposed class action in federal court in Brooklyn by three former Chili’s employees claims that New York’s policy, which most other US states share, allows Brinker to force employees to rely on tips and exposes them to unlawful discrimination.
“Brinker promotes a culture in which tipped service employees make customers ‘feel special,’ even at the expense of their dignity and safety,” the lawsuit says.
Brinker did not respond to a request for comment. The New York Attorney General’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the challenge to the state law.
Many worker advocates have for years called for the elimination of sub-minimum wages that companies may pay to workers who earn tips under federal and most state laws, as long as tips make up the difference.
In New York, where the minimum wage is $16 an hour or $17 in and around New York City, food service workers who earn tips may be paid $10.70 or $11.35 an hour. The federal tipped minimum wage is $2.13 an hour, compared with the traditional minimum wage of $7.25, and applies in states that do not set their own minimums.
RELYING ON TIPS
Advocates say that because tips are discretionary and unpredictable, they should supplement workers’ incomes rather than make up most of their pay. The lawsuit against Brinker says that relying on tips forces workers to tolerate conduct such as sexual harassment and customers’ potential racial bias.
The plaintiffs’ lawyers said in the lawsuit that they plan to expand the case to include a nationwide class of Chili’s workers.
Brinker operates more than 1,200 Chili’s restaurants in the US, including 36 in New York. The company also owns Maggiano’s Little Italy, an Italian restaurant chain with about 50 US locations.
The lawsuit claims that Chili’s reliance on customer ratings to determine workers’ schedules, shifts and table assignments is also unlawful. The ratings system can be racially biased, the lawsuit says, and can make it difficult for servers to reject unwanted advances from customers for fear of a poor rating.
The named plaintiffs, three former employees at a Chili’s in the Glendale section of Queens in New York City, claim they were routinely subjected to sexual advances and inappropriate comments and that management did not adequately protect workers from harassment.
(Reporting by Daniel Wiessner in Albany, New York, Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi and Rod Nickel)

A Washington contractor was fined $48,803 after a roofer was killed when he fell through a skylight.
Leslie & Campbell Inc. of Union Gap was fined $48,803 after a roofer fell more than 25 feet through an unguarded skylight to the concrete floor of a fruit packing warehouse in Wapato, according to the Washington State Department of Labor & Industries.
L&I cited the company after investigators found it had not guarded the skylight, identified skylights as a fall hazard or adequately trained workers on the danger.
The company is appealing the citation and fine.
L&I also issued penalties against other roofing companies and subcontractors in recent months:
- Roof Doctor Inc. of Olympia received the largest fine, $238,680, on June 30 for four willful serious and two serious fall protection violations. A portion of a roof collapsed beneath a worker in Tumwater, and inspectors determined his safety rope was too long to arrest his fall. The worker was hospitalized. Roof Doctor and its associated companies have been cited for more than 80 safety violations since 2004, including 34 for failing to ensure workers wore fall protection, according to L&I. The business is appealing the latest citation.
- Dabella/Reve Exteriors LLC of Marysville was fined $176,580 on Aug. 19 for two willful serious violations involving failure to protect subcontractor employees from falls and ensure they wore required protective equipment. Some violations repeated findings from earlier inspections, according to L&I. The company is appealing. Its subcontractor on the same job, Suruka House LLC, was fined $34,668 for repeatedly failing to ensure workers wore fall protection and other required protective equipment.
- Bartlett Homes & Roofing LLC of Veradale was fined $179,964 on June 3 for willful serious and repeat serious violations. Inspectors found two workers were not connected to a fall protection system, anchors were improperly installed and one worker’s fall restraint rope had enough slack that it would not have prevented him from hitting the ground. The company is appealing. Ivan’s Roofing Spokane LLC, a subcontractor on the same job, was fined $37,415 for workers not using fall protection, unsafe ladder use and failure to ensure first aid was available to injured workers.
- Money collected from fines goes into the workers’ compensation supplemental pension fund, which is earmarked to help injured workers and families of workers who died on the job.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is the hot topic on Wall Street and Main Street right now. But for those old enough to remember, the environment may be starting to feel like the dot-com bubble, which burst at the turn of the century. Companies like Oklo (OKLO +5.36%), NuScale Power (SMR +8.16%), and even Constellation Energy (CEG +2.57%) all fell around 7% from their highs over the last five days, as of this writing. Bloom Energy (BE +7.15%) is down 13% from its high in that shockingly short period.
Meanwhile, ExxonMobil (XOM -2.51%) and Chevron (CVX -1.63%) are hitting all-time highs. There's risk in all of these stocks, but I'd rather own the stocks where the risks are easier to see and understand. That means Exxon and Chevron would be my pick. Here's why.
What happens when the AI bubble bursts?
The capital spending going into artificial intelligence is massive. AI is just a computer program, so it needs electricity to operate. That should lead to strong demand for power. That's the basic story behind companies like Oklo, NuScale, Bloom Energy, and Constellation Energy.
Of the four, Oklo and NuScale are the most speculative. These two companies are attempting to build businesses around small modular nuclear reactors. The opportunity could be huge, but at this point both companies are losing money and haven't yet proven their technologies are financially viable. Only the most aggressive investors should be considering them.

Bloom is the more aggressive option, as investors have priced a lot of good news into the stock. Even after a material pullback, the price-to-earnings ratio is still over 100x. Constellation Energy is probably the best positioned to weather an AI pullback, given the long-term contracts it signs, but irrational investors tend to throw the baby out with the bathwater when things turn south. If the AI bubble bursts, all of these stocks are likely to be hard hit, and the pullback over the last week is a sign of the all-or-nothing approach investors often take with new technologies.

Shares of Procter & Gamble (PG) rose 5.6% on October 22, 2026, the day the company reported its fiscal first quarter of 2027, while the S&P 500 fell 1.2%. Organic sales, which leave out currency and acquisitions, grew faster than P&G forecasts for the full year. At the same time, management raised its estimate of what higher costs will take from earnings. Did either change P&G’s profit forecast for fiscal 2027?
Procter & Gamble Held Profit Forecast As Costs Rose
Management kept its fiscal 2027 forecast for core earnings per share, the company’s adjusted measure, at $6.89 to $7.11, the same range it gave in July. The company held this outlook while raising its estimate of the hit from input costs, currency and items below operating profit to about 11% of fiscal 2026 core earnings per share, up from 8% in July. P&G now plans to reach the same profit while absorbing a larger cost bill, and that is what the quarter changed.
During the first quarter, core earnings per share of $2.00 topped the consensus estimate of $1.94. Revenue came in a little light at $23.3 billion against the $23.5 billion expected. Even so, organic sales rose 4.0%, above the 1% to 3% organic growth P&G forecasts for the full year. Each of its 10 product categories grew.
The stock’s jump was not P&G’s alone. Over the same session, Colgate-Palmolive rose 4.3% and Church & Dwight 3.7%. Much of the day’s gain was shared with other household-goods makers, though P&G rose more than either.
Was Procter & Gamble Already Losing Margin?

Those days are over. “I’m so frustrated,” Stoneman said. “It’s like, what about all this ‘Drill, baby, drill’?”

Some 221 trucking companies have filed for bankruptcy so far this year, according to data compiled by Bloomberg, extending a three-year spike at sustained levels not seen in decades.
Around two-thirds of small US carriers — typically operating 20 or fewer tractors, and oftentimes only just one — report that revenue is either flat or down compared with the year-ago period, according to a survey of hundreds of such companies conducted over the past two months by freight-management firm Truckstop and Bloomberg Intelligence. A high-speed rail service slammed into another train about 60 miles south of Madrid on Wednesday, killing at least 64 people — the second major accident on Spain’s rail network this year and the deadliest crash in over a decade.
“We’re talking about an enormous death toll,” said Emiliano García Page, president of Castilla-La Mancha region, where the accident occurred. “Firefighters expect that more victims will still be found.”
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is traveling to the area as evacuation efforts continue.
The crash has become Spain’s most lethal railway catastrophe since 2013, when 80 people perished after a train derailed in the Galicia region, north of Madrid. Another collision this past January also killed more than 40 people, provoking intense scrutiny of Spain’s rail infrastructure — once seen as a point of national pride.
Both accidents this year happened on the line running south from Madrid and involved state-owned train operator Renfe and Iryo, a rival operator controlled by Italy’s state-owned company Ferrovie dello Stato.
Wednesday’s collision occurred just before 9 a.m. local time, when a Renfe high-speed train hit an Iryo train between the villages of Los Yébenes and Urda, according to an official at Spain’s railway infrastructure manager Adif. The impact derailed at least two carriages on the Iryo train, interrupting all traffic on the high-speed line between Madrid and Seville.
Local authorities quickly dispatched ambulances, helicopters, police and Red Cross personnel, while the Spanish government deployed the army’s Emergency Military Unit, a special task force for civilian disasters and accidents.
Several trains are now halted as Adif helps travelers reach stations.
A spokesperson for Spain’s Transportation Ministry said the initial assessment suggests human error, potentially by an Adif rail traffic controller, was to blame. The Adif official declined to comment on what might have caused the accident.
The crash is likely to become a major talking point in Spain’s upcoming national election on Nov. 29. Sanchez and several ministers canceled their appointments for the day, as did the opposition leader.
Even before the cause or death toll was known, Santiago Abascal, leader of the far-right Vox party, blamed the accident on the “abandonment, ruin and betrayal suffered by Spaniards” at the hands of Sánchez’s government.
Vox is polling third and could play a decisive role in forming the next government, with polls showing the conservative People’s Party in the lead.
Spain’s last major railway accident sparked a nationwide debate over the safety of the country’s nearly 4,000 kilometers of high-speed rail network, the world’s second-largest, according to the International Union of Railways.
That incident remains under investigation, but the opposition blames the government for neglecting infrastructure, from railways to roads.
Some 40 million people traveled on Spain’s commercial high-speed rail services in 2024, up 77% from 2019, according to data from the national competition authority. The increase partly reflects population growth as well as a surge in tourism, with Spain now receiving close to 100 million visitors a year.

Cost-of-living crisis
As a net energy importer, the U.K. is vulnerable to external energy shocks.
Inflation has risen sharply this year, with surging fuel costs driving the annual inflation rate to 3.5% in September. Markets expect the Bank of England to hike interest rates next month, while government borrowing costs have risen sharply this year.
The U.K. government, led by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, had promised to alleviate economic pressures ahead of the budget.
On Wednesday, Healey said he would deliver "breathing space" for families, saying the country needs "radical change on energy," and citing the inflationary impact of the U.S.-Iran war — a conflict he said "we did not want."
His measures included the removal of standing charges on household gas heating bills, the extension of a tax break on electricity for millions of households through July 2027, and £100 ($133) checks for those living in the four lowest local housing tax bands. This will cost £2.6 billion.
Healey said tariffs would be removed on over 100 grocery products, a policy announced before the budget was officially unveiled. Small business relief from business rates — a tax on commercial premises — would be extended to include more companies in the hospitality, retail and leisure sectors. Other measures included £15 million to provide books for children, funding aimed at reducing homelessness and support for people to purchase their first home.
The U.K.'s minimum wage will rise by 3.9%, while a planned cut to tax-free savings thresholds was canceled.

Bank of America's top technical strategist flagged a pattern that preceded every major market peak since 2000, and it is showing up again right now in the data investors use least.
At the end of September, Americans who borrow against their stocks owed their brokers about $1.48 trillion, close to a record. That debt has held up, but its growth has slowed sharply.
In a note dated October 23, 2026, Bank of America (NYSE:BAC | BAC Price Prediction) technical strategist Paul Ciana said year-over-year margin debt growth fell to 31.4% in September, down from 53.7% in May. He said that when growth cools off after an extreme run, the slowdown has lined up with past market peaks and can signal a top. He framed the slowdown as a warning sign of elevated risk.
Both the broad market and the retail broker rose after the warning. SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) rose 0.57% to 769.66 on October 27. Robinhood Markets (NASDAQ:HOOD) gained 1.85% to $94.56 on the same day it reported a record margin book that is growing much more slowly.
Why BofA Pays Attention to Slowing Growth
BofA ranked May’s growth rate fourth-highest since 1998. The only higher levels came in 2000, 2007 and 2021, and a stock decline followed each one.
The total itself is still rising. September balances rose 1.80% from August and sit 1.47% below June’s high. The growth rate, however, has fallen.
The pace matters more than the total because each new dollar of margin debt is new buying power. When that new borrowing slows, the market loses a source of demand. If prices then fall, margin calls (demands from brokers for more cash or collateral) push borrowers to sell into the decline. Riding a late-cycle rally is fine as long as the exit is planned, which is the whole subject of our free bubble survivor’s handbook.
Ciana raised this risk before. On June 29, with growth near 54%, he wrote that “U.S. equities could face a corrective phase in the third quarter.” He also pointed to an opposing pattern: “Typically, risk assets such as the S&P 500 rebound after midterms unless more severe downside risks materialize.”

Over one month, the ten largest leveraged equity ETFs took in $12 billion of new money while their market value fell $20 billion. The largest triple-leveraged semiconductor fund drew $9 billion in two weeks, the biggest two-week inflow in its history.
These funds borrow internally to deliver two or three times an index’s daily return, so investors get leverage without a margin loan showing up in brokerage data. Options work the same way, because a small premium controls a large position. Retail traders recently made up 61% of options volume on one large market maker’s platform.

Jon Mott set his marathon PR—a 2:17:20—on the famously flat and speedy course of the Berlin Marathon in 2022. Then, a few months later, he traveled to Boston for 26.2, feeling equally confident in his training, but was punished by the repeated hills and fell well short of his goal.
So what happened in Boston?
“At no point was I able to lock into my rhythm,” says Mott, a three-time U.S. Olympic Marathon Trials qualifier and run coach at Runnersfix. “There was no flow to the race, I guess you can say, and it just really beat me up.”
Over time, Mott came to see a pattern in his contrasting performances. On flat, rhythmic courses, he could open up his stride and cruise, letting his powerful gait carry him through the finish line with little interruption. But on hilly courses, he noticed runners, who could more easily shorten their stride and adjust their turnover, often seemed better equipped to handle the change of pace that comes with an undulating course.
Mott now uses this observation as a coaching lens with the runners he trains. He sees some athletes as more stride-oriented—like himself—and others as more cadence-oriented.
These designations aren’t fixed labels or an automatic explanation for every race result, but they offer a clue into a runner’s strengths and weaknesses. Generally, stride runners excel on flat courses but need more hill-specific preparation, while cadence runners tend to handle hills well but need more practice on flat terrain.
Here’s how to identify the pattern in your own running, why knowing your tendency could help you run your next race faster, and how to use this finding to prepare more intentionally for your next race.
Stride vs. Cadence Runner: What’s the Difference?
In Mott’s framework, stride runners succeed at fast paces by lengthening their stride while keeping their cadence relatively steady across all speeds. Cadence runners get faster mainly by taking more steps per minute, with a less pronounced change in stride length.
Mott first came across this distinction a few years ago while looking for a new racing shoe and comparing the 2024 edition of Asics’s Metaspeed Edge and Sky models. Drawing on data from its sports-science institute, Asics separated runners who primarily lengthen their stride as they speed up from those who primarily increase their step rate, Runner’s World previously reported. The company also found that stride runners tended to land closer to the midfoot or forefoot, while cadence runners more often had smoother turnover and favored more of a heel strike.
This helped Mott confirm the patterns he had noticed in his own races, and then he expanded that idea into his clients’ plans, using it to help figure out their strengths and where they might need more practice.

Cadence runners, in Mott’s view, flourish on courses with frequent changes in terrain. Because they rely more on step frequency to get faster, Mott believes they can more readily adjust their turnover. Essentially, their shorter, quicker steps make it easier to adapt to changes when the course may disrupt those with longer strides, he says.

On a rainy Saturday in June 2024, Hannah Zarzecki cried as she crossed the Grandma’s Marathon finish line. It was her eighth marathon, and despite following a training plan, she didn’t achieve her sub-4 goal—again. “I kept telling myself, ‘Why did I sign up for this? I still can’t PR. I’m freezing cold. My feet hurt,’” she says. “It was so miserable.”
She didn’t know that a chance encounter at that race was about to change that.
A high school cross-country runner, Zarzecki returned to the sport after graduating from Harvard University, where she played ice hockey. Wanting a goal to work toward, she entered the 2018 Chicago Marathon lottery and won a bib in her hometown race.
Leading up to the race, Zarzecki had not run more than about 15 miles and didn’t follow a training plan. She was in good shape from teaching spin classes several nights a week and wasn’t sure how else to prepare. I’m either gonna finish this marathon, or I am gonna end up in the hospital, she remembers thinking. She was surprised and proud when, taking walk breaks, she ran her way to the finish in 5:04:59.
Not convinced that marathons were for her, Zarzecki turned her focus to shorter distances, 10Ks and half marathons—until a spin class student told her about completing the Berlin Marathon. She loved the idea of traveling to run races in other countries, so she applied for and got into the same marathon. After loosely following a training plan she found online this time, she ran and walked the 2021 Berlin Marathon in 5:16:32. Disappointed, she decided to commit to working on her time.
Zarzecki found a coach on Instagram whom she paid to create a training plan for her. She devoted herself to this regimen, which included her first experience with speedwork and intervals. She also joined the Electric Athletic Club in Chicago and participated in their group runs.
Zarzecki raced the 2022 Rock ’n’ Roll Nashville Marathon. Without taking walking breaks, she finished in 4:12:11, improving her Berlin time by more than an hour seven months later. “When I actually put my mind to training and following this plan, everything kind of came together, and I’m like, ‘Oh, this is how you’re supposed to do a marathon,’” she says. She was hooked.
For the next couple of years, Zarzecki used the same training plan, running about 30 miles each week. In May 2023, she surprised herself on her 28th birthday when she finished the Wisconsin Marathon in 4:00:28.

Two tech behemoths -- Alphabet (GOOG +1.60%) (GOOGL +1.34%) and Microsoft (MSFT -0.06%) -- reported earnings today. Both showed strong cloud growth, but the market is treating them very differently. Microsoft shares popped after hours while Alphabet stock sank. Why?
I think a big part of the answer is how each plans to pay for the massive outlays both have planned.
Cloud growth accelerated at both companies
Microsoft beat Wall Street's targets with sales up 19%, reaching $92.3 billion. GAAP -- generally accepted accounting principles -- earnings per share (EPS) came in at $4.92. Adjusted EPS was $4.89, above the roughly $4.72 the Street expected. Azure, its cloud platform, grew 48%, reaching $33.17 billion in revenue.
Alphabet's cloud growth was even stronger than Microsoft's: 103% growth for the unit, earning $11.1 billion in operating income on $30.7 billion in sales. Overall, sales jumped 25%, reaching $127.6 billion, slightly missing estimates, while GAAP EPS actually fell from $2.87 to $2.12. Search and YouTube ads also underperformed.
Alphabet's cash flow is the real problem
Some of Alphabet's EPS drop can be explained by an $8.7 billion net loss on equity securities, but even if you remove this -- worth $0.55 per share -- the earnings still came in well below what Wall Street was looking for.
While it's not a great look, I think the real issue the market is reacting to is the company's cash picture. Alphabet spent $51.4 billion on capital expenditures (capex), up from $24.0 billion a year ago. Operating cash flow -- the cash the actual business generated -- was $42.3 billion. That left free cash flow (FCF) -- the money left after paying for its capex investments -- at negative $9.1 billion. That's worse than the negative $5.9 billion the company reported last quarter.
During the quarter, Alphabet raised $28.7 billion through senior unsecured notes and $12.4 billion from selling stock. Long-term debt has grown from $46.5 billion at the end of 2025 to $125.1 billion.
Alphabet said its capex guidance for 2026 holds -- $195 billion to $205 billion -- but said it expects capex in 2027 to "increase significantly."
Microsoft is still paying its own way
Microsoft, on the other hand, is still FCF positive, though like Alphabet, that figure is moving in the wrong direction. The company reported FCF of $18.63 billion, down 27% year over year, after $39.37 billion in cash capital spending. Its broader capex figure, which includes finance leases, was $45.2 billion.
CFO Amy Hood said on July's earnings call that the company expects to stay free-cash-flow positive for its current fiscal year, though capex is expected to expand. On that call, she also said demand for its cloud services was running ahead of supply.
The bottom line
Microsoft at this point has a much healthier cushion in its quarterly cash flow -- more room to keep spending while it waits for those investments to pay off. Alphabet is increasingly asking lenders and shareholders to help cover the bill.
Obviously, the growth is hard to argue with, but I still think the jury is out on whether this bet will pay off for both companies. Costs are climbing, and I'm concerned the math won't pencil out long

The US power sector would emit 2.1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide by 2030, after factoring in planned AI projects. That’s 618 million tons more than 2025 levels, by the Sierra Club’s calculations, or about a 42% increase.
A year and a half ago, researchers at the nonprofit environmental group would have estimated that the buildout and its impact would have been a quarter or half of current projections, said Jeremy Fisher, the Sierra Club’s principal advisor for climate and energy. “The numbers continue to sort of boggle our minds,” he said.
Many data center developers are turning to natural gas to meet the immense electricity demand, relying on power sources that are both on and off the grid. The bulk of the expected emissions by 2030 would come from sources that are not directly linked to the grid, often built by tech companies to avoid the long wait for a connection. These could exceed 460 million tons, Fisher said, roughly the same as the annual emissions of Mexico.
Helen Kou, a BloombergNEF analyst, said if there’s significant growth in gas power for new facilities, “you would presume emissions would increase from year to date.”
But how much is a difficult question to answer. There’s so much uncertainty in the projections for power emissions that the lowest and highest estimates differ by more electricity than the combined demand of California and Florida.
The Sierra Club’s estimate of the climate impacts of the data center buildout is higher than others released so far. The wide range of projections is due to questions around how many facilities will actually be built, what technologies they will ultimately use and how much renewable energy capacity comes online over the next few years.
The environmental nonprofit Union of Concerned Scientists in January projected that fossil-fuel-powered electricity for data centers could increase US power-sector emissions by 19% to 29%, or as much as 342 million tons a year by 2035. US and Canadian researchers in June published a journal article projecting a 28% rise in the sector’s emissions.

The Connecticut town of East Haven is appealing a federal district court ruling that rejected its claim for insurance coverage for a civil lawsuit and $11 million judgment against it regarding the closure of a local quarry in 2017 for political reasons.
The $11 million was awarded to quarry owners who alleged that the town interfered with their operations through various regulatory measures before eventually shutting it down through a series of cease-and-desist orders in 2017. The quarry owners sought damages in excess of $25 million for actions by the town and its officials they say violated their federal and state constitutional rights.
The town had two different liability insurers, Starr Indemnity and Liability, and Allied World Insurance. Both insurers disclaimed duties to defend and indemnify the town for the quarry owners’ civil case under the terms of their policies.
The town sued to force the insurers to defend and indemnify it for the quarry owners’ lawsuit. In September, the federal district court for Connecticut granted summary judgment to the two insurers. The district court found that neither insurer breached a duty to indemnify or defend. In the case of Starr, the actions taken by the officials that closed the quarry were taken outside of the policy period. In Allied World’s case, an exclusion for claims related to the “lack of due process” barred coverage.
On October 21, the town informed the court it would be appealing that district court decision and the final judgement to the Second Circuit Court of Appeals.
The underlying action brought against the town, former Mayor Joseph Maturo, Jr., a zoning official and the town tax assessor by the quarry was filed in June 2017. The plaintiffs were John Patton, One Barberry Real Estate Holding, LLC and Farm River Rock LLC, who owned and operated a quarry in East Haven.
According to their complaint, the town’s actions included reclassifying portions of the quarry as industrial land and taxing it at a higher rate than previously beginning in October 2015; informing Patton that blasting permits would not be granted in the months preceding the 2015 municipal election; and issuing three cease-and-desist orders between February and May 2017, the last of which instructed the owners to completely shut down their quarry operations.
A federal judge in a bench trial concluded that the town and officials infringed on the quarry owners’ constitutionally protected property right in an arbitrary and irrational manner, in violation of their Fourteenth Amendment substantive due process protections. The judge awarded damages of $9,465,832. The quarry owners moved to alter the judgment and were granted prejudgment interest and attorneys’ fees and costs, bringing the total to $11,000,000.

The U.S. government isn’t doing enough to fight the surge in cyberscams, and partnerships with the private sector remain fragmented and voluntary, an investigation into the global scam industry led by the Joint Economic Committee of the U.S. Congress has found.
The government doesn’t even have a unified accounting of how much money has been seized from overseas scam compounds, nor how much has been returned to victims, according to the report, released Tuesday by ranking Democrats Sen. Maggie Hassan and Rep. Don Beyer.
Support for Victims
Citing findings from a yearlong investigation into global scams by The Associated Press and FRONTLINE, the report called for greater collaboration across agencies, support for victims, and deeper private sector engagement.
“Transnational criminal organizations run massive compounds that exploit U.S. technology, including AI, to carry out scams against Americans with devastating consequences,” Hassan said in an email. “The scale of this exponentially growing challenge requires Congress, the Administration, and the private sector to all strengthen their efforts.”
The report, which the AP obtained before its release, made clear how hard it is for scam victims to get their money back, despite the quickening pace of seizures announced by a variety of U.S. government agencies.
The FBI told the committee that it returned $336 million to scam victims in 2025.
The Federal Trade Commission reported that it had returned $1.83 billion to fraud victims in fiscal year 2025, but couldn’t determine how much of that money had been lost to overseas scam compounds.
The U.S. Secret Service returned more than $770 million in seized assets to fraud victims in fiscal years 2024 and 2025, but noted the money had come from a range of fraud schemes.
The U.S. State Department said that foreign law enforcement agencies that receive support from the department had seized proceeds “in the low hundreds of millions of dollars,” but told Congress to ask the Departments of Justice, Homeland Security and Treasury for details.
Taken together, that only adds up to a fraction of what victims have lost. Americans reported cyberfraud losses of nearly $18 billion — that’s more than $2 million an hour — last year to the FBI. Many don’t even report the crime.

Twenty-one US states and the District of Columbia sued President Donald Trump’s administration on Tuesday over its rollback of reporting requirements established under a 2021 law aimed at combating illicit finance.
The Trump administration in August finalized a rule exempting US companies and individuals from reporting beneficial ownership information to the Treasury Department’s financial crimes unit, rolling back reporting requirements established under the 2021 Corporate Transparency Act.
In their lawsuit, the coalition of mostly Democratic-led states asked a federal court to overturn the rule, which was part of a broader push by the Trump administration to curtail anti-corruption efforts.
“The executive branch cannot repeal a law by rulemaking. That fundamental principle resolves this case,” said the lawsuit filed in the US District Court for the District of Oregon.
The lawsuit said that the Trump administration effectively gutted the 2021 law by exempting more than 99.9% of companies originally required to disclose information about their owners.
The suit was filed against US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, the Department of the Treasury and its anti-money laundering Financial Crimes Enforcement Network.
The Treasury Department did not respond to a request for comment.
Bessent had cast the rule when it was made in August as “eliminating a burdensome reporting requirement for millions of law-abiding business owners without compromising our national security.”
The lawsuit also listed the heads of the US Departments of Justice and Homeland Security as defendants.
“The Trump administration has effectively overturned this law by enacting a rule that exempts all domestic companies and US owners of foreign companies from the law’s requirements, allowing the true owners of both foreign and domestic shell companies to remain anonymous,” New York Attorney General Letitia James, who was among the more than 20 state attorneys general who filed the challenge, said in a statement.
US Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs Committee, said in August that rolling back the reporting requirements increased the risks of sanctions evasion, fraud and drug trafficking, as well as sex trafficking and organized criminal activity.

A catastrophic 2025 Los Angeles firestorm exposed some 7 million people to high levels of airborne lead and other toxic metals released from burning homes and vehicles, according to a new study.
Scientists for the first time were able to quantify in real time the chemical composition of wildfire smoke thanks to a sensor network that went online months before the January 2025 Eaton conflagration that destroyed more than 9,400 buildings, killing 19 people.
Related: Will California’s New Smoke Claims Law Create a Recovery Bottleneck?
As climate change triggers urban firestorms like the inferno in the LA suburb of Altadena, the paper published Wednesday in the journal Science Advances offers the first indication of how the incineration of homes, electronics, cars and infrastructure could affect even people who live far from the burn zone due to wind-blown toxic smoke.
The researchers determined that over a 24-hour period, smoke from the fire contained 80 times the concentration of lead normally found in the atmosphere. Lead is a neurotoxin linked to an array of health effects and is particularly harmful to children. Sensors also detected highly elevated levels of arsenic and other toxins. The smoke plume covered eastern LA and the San Gabriel Valley and affected about 70% of the county’s population.
Nga Lee (Sally) Ng, a co-author of the study and a professor of environmental science and engineering at the California Institute of Technology, said that while chronic exposure to metals like lead is well-studied, the health effects from short-term exposure to highly concentrated airborne toxins remains largely unknown.
“The hope is that with these real-time measurements, we can better understand and characterize the health impacts of these short-term exposures,” she said.
The data on Eaton was collected by a Los Angeles monitoring site that happened to be downwind of the fire. It’s part of the Atmospheric Science and Chemistry Measurement Network (ASCENT) that has established stations across the country. Ng, who is a principal investigator for the National Science Foundation-funded project, said the LA site wasn’t able to collect data on the Palisades fire, which ignited 34 miles away from the Eaton site hours earlier, due to the wind direction.
Related: Edison Drops on Willful Misconduct Allegations in Eaton Fire Case
ASCENT also allowed the researchers to track how the toxic composition of the smoke plume changed over time as the fire burned, according to Haroula Baliaka, the study’s lead author who was a PhD candidate at Caltech at the time. That could help health researchers pinpoint health impacts from urban firestorms.
She said the study results should encourage policymakers to rethink strategies for evacuating residents from urban wildfires, given toxic smoke exposure can occur far from the burn zone. “I can envision that in the future we have these evacuation zones for smoke exposure as well,” said Baliaka. “Unfortunately, this is not a one-time event. It’s a new reality and we need to adapt to it and we need to do it sooner rather than later.”

Jim Cramer Says Chevron Beats Exxon. Earnings Will Put That to the Test
Jim Cramer told Mad Money viewers to swap Exxon for Chevron, and on October 30 both giants report back to back. Six numbers will reveal whether that call holds or collapses.
ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM | XOM Price Prediction) and Chevron (NYSE:CVX) both report third-quarter results before the open on October 30. Because the two reports land back to back, they give a clean test of Jim Cramer’s October 15 call on Mad Money.
“I think Exxon’s good. I think Chevron’s better. I would make that swap unless you have some tax implications. CVX is a better way to go,” Cramer said. This year, the two stocks have moved almost in tandem. Exxon is up 48.4% year to date, and Chevron is up 47.0%.
Chevron Absorbed the Middle East Shock Better
Darren Woods, Exxon’s board chair and chief executive, reported second-quarter earnings of $14.5 billion and operating cash flow of $23.6 billion, even though the Middle East conflict temporarily knocked out about 10% of upstream production. Woods also pointed to Guyana output near 900,000 barrels per day, record Permian volumes above 1.8 million oil-equivalent barrels per day, more than $9 billion returned to shareholders, and $16.3 billion in cumulative cost savings since 2019. “Stepping back, the second quarter was shaped by disruption, but defined by execution,” he said.
Chevron CFO Eimear Bonner reported adjusted EPS of $6.06 and adjusted free cash flow (the cash left over after capital spending) of $15.4 billion, with only about 1% of production affected by the conflict. Mike Wirth, who spoke as chair and CEO, cited record U.S. upstream output of nearly 2.1 million barrels of oil equivalent per day and $3 billion in structural cost cuts reached six months early. “Amid geopolitical uncertainty and market volatility, Chevron delivered a strong second quarter,” Wirth said.
Wall Street Expects Earnings to More Than Double
Quarterly growth figures compare with year-ago adjusted EPS of $1.88 for Exxon and $1.85 for Chevron.
Lost Barrels, a Fifth FPSO, and Project Kilby
For Exxon, three things matter:
- Whether the lost Middle East production has come back
- When Guyana’s fifth FPSO (a floating production, storage, and offloading vessel) starts up
- How chemical and refining margins held up
Power is Chevron’s key variable. Jeff Gustavson, president of Chevron New Energies, described a 20-year take-or-pay deal to supply Project Kilby, a Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) project, with 2.67 gigawatts of behind-the-meter power, meaning electricity generated on site for the customer. A final investment decision is expected later this year. Benefits from the Hess acquisition also matter, along with progress toward Bonner’s goal of 2% to 3% annual production growth through 2030.
Skeptics have a case. A guest on CNBC’s Fast Money said that oil services stocks have lagged so far behind the majors that Exxon and Chevron look “increasingly extended.” A Halftime Report panelist pushed back, citing Saudi Aramco’s view that rebuilding global inventories could take two years or more. The Cardinals have three finalists: second baseman JJ Wetherholt, shortstop Masyn Winn and pitcher Michael McGreevy.
McGreevy was a surprise contender, but he shouldn’t have been. The Cardinals raved about his defensive ability all year, and his glove is seen as a real contributing factor to his success on the mound, which included a roughly league-average 3.95 ERA despite a strikeout rate that ranked in just the ninth percentile. McGreevy’s 5 Defensive Runs Saved put him in a tie for second among all pitchers behind, oddly, Braves reliever Brent Suter. McGreevy would be an unlikely winner, though, if just because of name recognition: His competitors are the Braves’ Chris Sale and the Mets’ Nolan McLean.
Wetherholt and Winn as finalists were much less surprising. Winn won a Gold Glove in 2025, and he was first among National League shortstops again in DRS and Statcast’s Outs Above Average (OAA) in 2026. Winn is up against the Diamondbacks’ Geraldo Perdomo and the Cubs’ Dansby Swanson, and he’s probably the favorite to win it again. If so, he’ll only have … 11 to go to catch Ozzie Smith.
Wetherholt might be even more deserving. He was in the 100th percentile in OAA and Statcast’s fielding run value, and some metrics had him as the best defender in baseball. One of those metrics, however, is not DRS, where he’s tied for second among NL second basemen, behind the Brewers’ Brice Turang, one of his competitors for this award (along with the Pirates’ Brandon Lowe). Turang has already won one Gold Glove, and, considering his importance to the Brewers’ success this year, one might consider him the favorite to do it again. If Wetherholt wins this, there’s no question it will be the first of many.
Rookie of the Year Award
Finalists announced Monday, winners Nov. 9
For most of the year, Wetherholt was considered the favorite for this award, but his bat faded down the stretch, including a .307 OBP after the All-Star break. That allowed the Reds’ Sal Stewart and the Mets’ McLean and Carson Benge to gain on him and, arguably, pass him.
Still, there’s a great statistical case to be made for Wetherholt. Along with the Cubs’ Pete Crow-Armstrong, he might have been the best defensive player in the sport this year (at least by Outs Above Average). Wetherholt’s WAR lead over Stewart is dramatic: 4.6 to 2.0, according to FanGraphs. Wetherholt’s offensive numbers were suppressed by his home park, while Stewart’s, fair to say, were not. Stewart’s baseball-card numbers might end up earning him the nod, but even with the second-half fade, it’s hard to argue Wetherholt doesn’t deserve serious consideration.

Missouri passed a law to compensate the wrongfully convicted. Now it doesn’t want to pay.
Two men are seeking $2.4 million for their combined 38 years lost in prison. The attorney general is fighting them in court.
Dale Helmig is seeking compensation for the more than 14 years he spent wrongfully incarcerated in Missouri (Katie Moore/Marshall Project).
After Missouri lawmakers expanded eligibility for wrongfully convicted people to receive compensation last year, Dale Helmig thought he could get nearly $1 million for the more than 14 years he spent in prison. And Darryl Burton hoped to obtain more than $1.5 million for the 24-plus years he was incarcerated.
But today, they are back in the legal system that put them away. The state attorney general is arguing in court that the two men aren’t innocent, setting aside judges’ prior decisions — and that even if they were, the new law isn’t retroactive.
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway’s effort to fight their compensation requests — the first two under the new compensation law — is part of a long history of the office vigorously opposing innocence claims. Under her predecessors, attorneys there have kept people in prison even after a judge has ordered their release and continued to fight cases in the face of overwhelming evidence of innocence.
Peter Joy, a law professor at Washington University in St. Louis, said the Attorney General’s Office “has opposed claims of innocence on a very consistent basis, even though there have been times when the local prosecutor’s offices have recognized that the person had a valid claim of innocence.”
That doesn’t necessarily mean they aren’t examining each case on its merits, Joy said. But if they were opposing these without a “good faith basis,” it would be a violation of prosecutors’ ethical obligation to seek justice, he said. A spokesperson for Hanaway declined to comment, citing the pending cases.
When Helmig and Burton were released from prison, only those exonerated through DNA evidence qualified for state compensation — not people like them, whose convictions were overturned based on recantations or other types of newly discovered evidence.
Then, last year, the Missouri legislature expanded eligibility and increased the amount of money exonerees can collect. The measure was approved by Gov. Mike Kehoe.
The law allocates about $65,000 for every year of wrongful incarceration. That amount is paid on an annual basis, not as a lump sum.
In Helmig’s case, a judge in DeKalb County, about an hour north of Kansas City, ruled in 2010 that there was clear and convincing evidence that he was innocent.
Helmig had been convicted in the 1993 murder of his mother, Norma, whose body was found in a river in central Missouri, near where she lived. Prosecutors said his motive was a dispute over a phone bill, and that he’d thrown her purse from the bridge he would have traveled on from her home on the night of the murder.
But uncovered evidence implicated Helmig’s father, court records show. The couple were in divorce proceedings. Helmig’s father had access to her mail at a local post office, including a canceled check that was dated after her death and later found in the purse. That undermined the prosecution’s theory about when the purse had been discarded — a key detail in their case against Helmig.
A state trooper also recanted his testimony. During the trial, he had told jurors that Helmig had not denied killing his mother when, in fact, he had.

Burnout among Missouri’s doctors, lawyers and executives rarely announces itself. It shows up as a surgeon in Kansas City who stops sleeping through the night, a litigator in Clayton who adds a second drink most evenings, a hospital administrator in Springfield who snaps at a staff meeting and spends the drive home replaying it. Their work stays excellent. That is exactly the problem.
I am a licensed clinical social worker, and the people I see most often in this situation are not short on money, insurance or information. They are short on one thing: a way to get help that nobody at work will ever hear about.
The research on attorneys makes that point more clearly than anything else I know. The largest study of lawyer mental health, published in the Journal of Addiction Medicine in 2016, screened 12,825 licensed, employed attorneys. When the authors asked why people had not sought help, the two most common answers were not wanting others to find out and concerns about privacy or confidentiality. Among attorneys who had been in treatment, about half named the first reason.
That finding has held up. A 2026 research paper by my firm, CEREVITY, works through the decade of studies that followed and notes that the headline numbers vary with the method used. The fear of exposure is the one finding that shows up every time someone asks the question, in attorneys and in law students alike.
Doctors and senior executives carry the same calculation. A physician wonders who at the hospital will see the claim. A chief financial officer pictures the board hearing about it. A partner thinks about origination credit and what the firm did the last time someone admitted they were struggling. Each person decides, usually quickly and usually alone, that the safer move is to wait.
Here is what that waiting looks like in practice, in a composite drawn from common patterns rather than any one person. A Kansas City executive notices in January that she is lying awake at 3 a.m. By spring she is canceling lunches and rereading emails four times before sending them. By late summer a colleague asks if she is OK, and she says she is just busy. She finally calls someone in the fall, after a panic attack in a parking garage. The care she gets then is harder and slower than it would have been in January.
Missouri already has a piece of the answer, and it deserves more attention. The Missouri Bar’s lawyers’ assistance program offers counseling and referrals to every lawyer and judge in the state at no cost, and the Bar states plainly that its services are confidential and that reaching out does not affect a lawyer’s license. That last sentence matters more than any brochure. It answers the exact question that keeps people away.
Three changes would extend that logic beyond the bar.
First, employers should say the confidentiality promise out loud, in writing and from the top. A benefit nobody trusts is a benefit nobody uses. If a hospital system, law firm or company in St. Louis or Kansas City offers counseling, its leaders should spell out who can see what, and who cannot.

European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde will step down on Feb. 7 next year, she announced Thursday, formally kicking off a succession race that will be shaped by political bargaining and France's looming fiscal crisis.
Lagarde has led the central bank since July 2019, steering its responses to the Covid-19 pandemic, the Russia-Ukraine war and a series of energy price shocks that sent inflation in the European Union above 11% in 2022 and spurred the end of the post-Financial Crisis era of negative interest rates.
Lagarde will depart nearly nine months before her term was due to expire in October 2027, while the process to appoint her successor will begin immediately.
What the ECB is looking for in a successor
Senior ECB figures are already in talks about filling other senior roles, with chief economist Philip Lane and influential executive board member Isabel Schnabel, responsible for market operations, also due to step down next year.
The ECB is institutionally independent, and its Governing Council comprises the six-member Executive Board and the governors of the 21 euro area national central banks.
But appointments to its top jobs are made by the European Council following consultations with the European Parliament and euro area member states, with negotiations generally reflecting political bargaining over national representation and influence.
Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot, who both led their respective central banks for recent stints, are widely regarded as top contenders to replace Lagarde.
De Cos served from 2018 to 2024 and is now general manager of the Bank for International Settlements. Knot was Dutch central bank chief from 2011 until 2025 and is a distinguished visiting fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics.
The appointment of a new president is seen as crucial amid market debate over whether the ECB could use one of its intervention mechanisms as France faces a mounting sovereign debt crisis.
France's presidential election, due next year, is injecting further uncertainty as the country's bond yields spike and its spread over euro area benchmark Germany's rises to the highest level since the bloc's Sovereign Debt Crisis of the early 2010s.
Berenberg Chief Economist Holger Schmieding said that as a result, the ECB would need to consider who was best placed to deal with potential financial turbulence.
"As a former chair of the G20's Financial Stability Board (FSB), Knot may have an edge in this respect," Schmieding said in a note.
